# NGC 2683: A Galaxy in the Catalog

NGC 2683 can be described in a few numbers: an optical outline 8.71 by 2.57 arcminutes, a position angle of 44 degrees, and coordinates in the northern sky. Those measurements make it possible to locate and characterize the object, but they also show what a catalog can—and cannot—tell us about a galaxy.

The figures come from [NGC 2683’s entry in SIMBAD](https://simbad.cds.unistra.fr/simbad/sim-id?Ident=NGC%202683), an astronomical database that gathers classifications and measurements. Its listed angular dimensions describe the object’s apparent extent on the sky, not its physical size. The longer measurement is about 3.4 times the shorter one, so NGC 2683 appears distinctly elongated in this cataloged optical measurement. That alone does not establish the galaxy’s exact orientation in space.

SIMBAD records the measurement’s position angle as 44 degrees and marks its quality as D. In the database’s notation, D indicates a measurement uncertainty of 1 to 10 arcseconds. These details are useful reminders that catalog values are measurements with specified precision, not perfectly exact descriptions.

The same entry gives the galaxy’s J2000 coordinates as right ascension 8 hours, 52 minutes, 41.3 seconds and declination +33 degrees, 25 minutes, 18.6 seconds. Coordinates offer a more precise way to identify the target than its name alone. They are not a forecast of when it will be visible from a particular location; observing circumstances depend on where and when an observer looks.

Classification adds another layer of information. SIMBAD lists NGC 2683 as an active galaxy nucleus, with an object-type entry associated with a 2011 *Astronomy & Astrophysics* reference. Separately, its morphological type is recorded as SA, with the catalog citing a 2019 *Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society* paper. These labels describe different catalog categories. The entry itself does not explain the galaxy’s central activity or provide a detailed account of its structure.

The database also lists a radial velocity of about 411 kilometers per second and a spectroscopic redshift of 0.001372, drawing on a 2020 *Astrophysical Journal* reference. Those are distinct ways of reporting information about the galaxy’s motion and observed spectrum. They should not be confused with its sky coordinates or apparent angular size; each value answers a different kind of question.

Photometric measurements provide still another view. SIMBAD lists U, B, V and R magnitudes of 11.57, 10.68, 9.79 and 9.38, respectively, in the AB system. It also includes measurements in other filters, including J, H and K. These entries show that NGC 2683 has been measured across multiple wavelength bands, but the numbers are not a portrait of the galaxy by themselves. Their meaning depends on the filter and magnitude system specified in the catalog.

Taken together, the entry presents NGC 2683 not as a single striking image, but as an object described through coordinates, classifications, angular measurements, motion and light recorded in different bands. The elongated outline is one clear clue, while the other catalog fields supply separate pieces of context. Keeping those measurements distinct is the best way to read the record: a compact set of evidence about a distant galaxy, with each number telling only the part it measures.
